d92fa9b688d6.title: Catch-up Rules
d92fa9b688d6.content: . UNEPI’s catch-up schedule is summarised as “It is better to vaccinate late than never!”. | Dose | When to give | When not to give | . | Hepatitis B birth dose | As soon as possible after birth, ideally within 24 hours and up to 7 days | Not after 7 days | . | BCG | As soon as possible after birth | – | . | 6-week doses: OPV1, PCV1, DTP1, RV1, IPV1 | At 6 weeks, or as soon as possible thereafter | RV1: not after 2 years of age | . | 10-week doses: OPV2, PCV2, DTP2, RV2 | At 10 weeks, or as soon as possible thereafter, and at least 4 weeks after dose 1 | Not before 4 weeks have passed since the previous dose. RV2: not after 2 years of age | . | 14-week doses: OPV3, PCV3, DTP3, RV3, IPV2 | At 14 weeks, or as soon as possible thereafter, and at least 4 weeks after dose 2 | Not before 4 weeks have passed since the previous dose. RV3: not after 2 years of age | . | 9-month doses: MR1, YF | At 9 months, or as soon as possible thereafter | Not before 9 months of age (except where indicated) | . | MR2 | At 18 months, or as soon as possible thereafter, and at least 4 weeks after the previous dose | Not before 4 weeks have passed since MR1 | . General rules: . | Even if a long time has passed between doses, there is no need to restart the series from the beginning. | There is no upper age limit for most vaccines, except rotavirus (under 2 years) and the hepatitis B birth dose (under 7 days). | . How the logic encodes the catch-up rules . For a dose n > 1 with scheduled age an and minimum interval i = 4 weeks, the due date is . due(n) = max( date of birth + an, date of dose n−1 + i ). A dose is due when its due date is on or before today, upcoming when it is in the future, and expired when today is after its expiration (the last date on which the dose may be given). Expirations: . | hepatitis B birth dose: date of birth + 7 days; | OPV0: date of birth + 1 week (WHO value; Uganda does not state one, see open questions); | rotavirus: the day before the 2nd birthday; | HPV: the day before the 21st birthday (WHO single-dose age range; Uganda does not state one). | . The UNEPI catch-up chart lists “IPV1” at both 6 and 14 weeks; this guide reads the 14-week dose as IPV2, consistent with the routine schedule. Edit this page on GitHub .

0c671d6cff1d.title: Scheduling Logic
0c671d6cff1d.content: . The Uganda scheduling logic is the WHO DAK’s own scheduling logic, adapted where the Uganda schedule differs. It is built the way the WHO immunization DAK builds it (IG Starter Kit; litlfred/smart-immunizations tools/antigenchecklist.md): . | L2, the workbook. input/decision-logic/IMMZ DAK_decision-support logic.xlsx is a copy of the WHO DAK workbook. Uganda changes only the cells of the scheduling tables (IMMZ.D18.S.*) listed below. Each changed row’s Comments cell names the Uganda L1 statements it rests on (library/l1-recommendation-scenarios/uganda/). | L3, generated. WHO’s converter tools/node/processDTSchedule.js turns each adapted table into a PlanDefinition and its Library (input/fsh/plandefinitions/, input/fsh/libraries/; npm run logic:generate, checked on every pull request). | L3, completed. Each adapted CQL library is WHO’s finished library of the same name, with only the definitions whose cells changed rewritten, each marked // Uganda: with its L1 key. The new Td table’s library is the converter’s skeleton, completed from its pseudocode on WHO’s DTP data elements. | . Every other WHO table is used unchanged from the WHO IG this guide depends on. The full record, one row per table with its decision and evidence, is input/l2/dependencies.yaml. Adapted and added tables . | WHO table | Uganda change | L1 | . | IMMZ.D18.S.Hepatitis B.Birth dose schedule | expires at birth + 7 days | C01, C08 | . | IMMZ.D18.S.Polio.bOPV plus IPV schedule | IPV dose 1 at 6 weeks, IPV dose 2 at 14 weeks | S03, S07 | . | IMMZ.D18.S.DTP.On-time start schedule | primary series only (6, 10, 14 weeks); booster rows not generated — review pending | S04 | . | IMMZ.D18.S.Measles.Ongoing transmission schedule | MCV2 at 18 months, at least 4 weeks after MCV1 | S08, P09, C07, C13 | . | IMMZ.D18.S.Malaria schedule | doses at 6, 7, 8 and 18 months | S10, P05–P07, P09 | . | IMMZ.D18.S.HPV.Single-dose schedule | girls, at 10 years | P10, S13 | . | UG.IMMZ.D18.S.DTP.Td women of childbearing age schedule (new) | Td 1 at first contact, then 1, 6, 12 and 12 months — review pending | P11–P15, S14 | . Reused unchanged . BCG, polio birth dose, Hib 3 doses, pneumococcal 3 doses, rotavirus (WHO already expires every dose at 24 months, which is the Uganda rule C09–C11), rubella high-incidence (one dose from 9 months, given as MR1) and yellow fever. Configuration . Two Uganda rules are values of parameters the WHO libraries already expose; they are configured, not forked: . | WHO parameter | Library | WHO default | Uganda | L1 | . | HepBLowerLimitWeeks | IMMZD2DTHepatitisBEncounterElements (used by the 3- and 4-dose schedules) | 4 | 6 | S04, P02, C03 | . | HepBBirthDoseAgeLimitDays | IMMZD2DTHepatitisBElements (birth-dose eligibility) | 1 | 7 | C01, C08 | . Not in scope . Vitamin A and deworming are not vaccines and are outside the WHO immunization DAK (review item 6). Contraindications (IMMZ.D5.DT.*) and the eligibility tables (IMMZ.D2.DT.*) are WHO’s, unchanged. See open questions. Edit this page on GitHub .

576bb19b16c5.content: . Comparison of the Uganda routine schedule with the generic WHO scheduling logic in the WHO Immunization implementation guide (libraries IMMZD18S*Logic). “Same” means the Uganda rule falls within the WHO recommendation; the remaining rows are the adaptations this guide makes. | Vaccine | WHO (generic) | Uganda | Adaptation | . | BCG | 1 dose at birth | 1 dose at birth | Same | . | Hepatitis B birth dose | At birth; overdue after 24 hours; upper limit left to Member States | At birth, ideally within 24 hours, not after 7 days | Upper limit set to 7 days | . | OPV0 (bOPV birth dose) | At birth; IG expiration 1 week | At birth | WHO 1-week expiration kept (open question) | . | OPV1–3 | 3 bOPV doses from 6 weeks, at least 4 weeks apart | 6, 10, 14 weeks, at least 4 weeks apart | Same, with fixed scheduled ages | . | IPV | IPV1 from 14 weeks, IPV2 at least 4 months later | IPV1 at 6 weeks, IPV2 at 14 weeks, at least 4 weeks apart | Earlier IPV1 and shorter interval | . | DTP-HepB-Hib | 3 primary doses from 6 weeks, at least 4 weeks apart; 3 diphtheria–tetanus boosters (12–23 months, 4–7 years, 9–15 years) and a pertussis booster (1–6 years) | 3 primary doses at 6, 10, 14 weeks; no childhood boosters | Boosters not in the Uganda schedule | . | PCV | 3p+0 or 2p+1 | 3p+0 at 6, 10, 14 weeks | 3p+0 chosen | . | Rotavirus | From 6 weeks, at least 4 weeks apart, number of doses by product; IG expiration 24 months | 3 doses at 6, 10, 14 weeks; not after 2 years | 3-dose product schedule | . | Measles-rubella | MCV1 at 9 months (12 months in low transmission settings); MCV2 from 15 months | MR1 at 9 months, MR2 at 18 months | MR2 at 18 months | . | Yellow fever | 1 dose from 9 months in endemic areas | 1 dose at 9 months, nationwide | Same | . | Malaria | 4 doses, first from 5 months, at least 4 weeks apart; dose 4 about 12–18 months after dose 3 | 6, 7, 8 and 18 months | First dose at 6 months; dose 4 at 18 months of age (about 10 months after dose 3 when on time) | . | HPV | Single dose from 9 years (9–14 primary target; up to 20 years) | 1 dose for girls at 10 years | Scheduled age 10 years; WHO upper age kept (open question) | . | Td, women of child-bearing age | Tetanus-diphtheria in pregnancy (IG libraries IMMZD18SDTPPregnancy*) and childhood/adolescent boosters | 5 doses for women aged 15–49: first contact, +1 month, +6 months, +12 months, +12 months | Uganda 5-dose schedule for all women of child-bearing age | . Data model notes . | The Uganda logic reuses the WHO data elements (IMMZEncounterElements) and vaccine value sets (IMMZConcepts); no new value sets are introduced. | The WHO value set DTP-containing vaccines (IMMZ.Z.DE24) also lists Td (ATC J07AM51). The Uganda logic therefore counts a pentavalent dose only when the vaccine is also in Pertussis-containing vaccines (IMMZ.Z.DE12), and counts a Td dose only when it is not pertussis-containing. This may be worth raising with the WHO guide. | Birth doses (hepatitis B, OPV0) are recognised either by the WHO “Dose 0” series marker or by being given before 6 weeks of age, the minimum age of the infant primary series. | . Edit this page on GitHub .

8a5edab28263.title: Immunizations - Uganda adaptation (draft)
8a5edab28263.content: . This implementation guide is a draft adaptation of the WHO SMART Guidelines Immunization implementation guide to the Uganda routine immunisation schedule of the Uganda National Expanded Programme on Immunisation (UNEPI). It is prepared for review with UNEPI and is not an official publication of the Uganda Ministry of Health. What this guide adds to the WHO guide . The WHO guide gives generic, Member-State-adaptable content: data elements, decision logic and scheduling logic for every WHO-recommended vaccine. This guide keeps all of that and adds the Uganda-specific layer: . | the Uganda routine immunisation schedule and catch-up rules, as published by the Ministry of Health and presented by UNEPI; | routes and sites of administration used in Uganda; | a line-by-line comparison with the WHO recommendations; | computable scheduling logic: the WHO DAK’s scheduling tables, adapted cell by cell in a copy of the WHO DAK workbook and converted with WHO’s own toolchain, with two WHO parameters configured for Uganda, and test patients in the WHO test format; | the UNEPI user requirements for an electronic immunization registry and the service delivery and data flow context; | open questions where the Uganda sources are silent or ambiguous and a decision by UNEPI is needed. | . Sources . | Uganda Ministry of Health, Uganda Routine Immunisation Schedule (poster), attached to issue #1. | UNEPI, User requirements – SMART Guidelines (presentation), attached to issue #1: current immunisation schedule, catch-up schedule, sites of child vaccines, service points, client flow, data flow, current challenges and user requirements for an electronic immunization registry (EIR). | WHO, Immunization implementation guide (smart.who.int.immunizations), and WHO recommendations for routine immunization – summary tables. | . Where the L1 and L2 content is . The guide follows the SMART Guidelines layers: L1 is the guideline sources and the recommendations taken from them; L2 is the DAK components built on them. Most L2 components are reused from the WHO immunization DAK, as recorded in input/l2/dependencies.yaml. | layer | content | where | . | L1 | The two ingested sources: the MoH schedule poster and the UNEPI deck | library: poster, deck | . | L1 | Authored recommendations (53), with their mapping to the WHO vocabulary | L1 recommendations and scenarios; source library/l1-recommendation-scenarios/uganda/ | . | L2 | User-scenario candidates (53) | L1 recommendations and scenarios; source …/uganda/candidates/ | . | L2 | Decision logic: scheduling tables, adapted | Scheduling logic, Testing, Artifacts; workbook input/decision-logic/ | . | L2 | Personas, business processes, data elements | reused unchanged from the WHO immunization DAK | . | L2 | Functional and non-functional requirements | UNEPI user requirements; the 14 rows as smart-base FunctionalRequirement / NonFunctionalRequirement instances in input/fsh/requirements/ | . | L2 | Indicators | WHO indicators reused; the Uganda target-population denominators are not yet authored | . Status . Draft. Everything marked as an open question needs confirmation by UNEPI before the logic is used for clinical decision support. Edit this page on GitHub .

edd7fd170aad.title: UNEPI User Requirements
edd7fd170aad.content: . Requirements from the UNEPI presentation User requirements – SMART Guidelines. They are recorded here as stated, so they can later be mapped to the WHO guide’s functional and non-functional requirements. Each row of the two requirement tables below is also a DAK component 8 instance (smart-base FunctionalRequirement or NonFunctionalRequirement), with the same id, in input/fsh/requirements/. The deck states no actor (“as a”) and no benefit (“so that”) for them, so none is recorded. Programme . | Vision: a Ugandan population free of vaccine-preventable diseases. | Mission: to ensure that every child and high-risk group is fully vaccinated with high-quality and effective vaccines against the target diseases according to recommended strategies. | Goal: to contribute to the overall objective of the Health Sector Development Plan in reducing morbidity, mortality and disability due to vaccine-preventable diseases, so that they are no longer of public health importance. | Objectives: increase access and demand for immunization services; ensure availability of potent and effective vaccines; build EPI management capacity at all levels; monitor disease trends and programme performance; formulate policy, standards and guidelines. | . Current challenges (paper-based system) . High printing costs; delays in service delivery (time consuming); less accurate data; false zero-dose children (ZDC) and immunization under-coverage (IUC); no flexibility; no real-time processes; vaccine accountability. Expected benefits of digitization . Improved data quality; reminders; savings on printing; support for follow-up; identification of real defaulters; improved data use; improved visibility. Functional requirements for an electronic immunization registry (EIR) . | Id | Requirement | Detail | . | UG-FR-01 | User authentication and access control | Username/password, biometric authentication | . | UG-FR-02 | Patient record management | Personal information, vaccination history and demographic data | . | UG-FR-03 | Vaccine inventory management | Batch numbers, expiration dates and current stock | . | UG-FR-04 | Vaccination scheduling and reminders | Scheduling of vaccination appointments and reminders to patients or guardians | . | UG-FR-05 | Immunization reporting and analytics | Reports such as immunization coverage rates, vaccine wastage and adverse event tracking | . | UG-FR-06 | Adverse event reporting | Report and document adverse events following immunization (AEFI) | . | UG-FR-07 | Integration with health records | Integrate with existing electronic health record systems for comprehensive patient health information | . UG-FR-04 is supported directly by the scheduling logic of this guide. Non-functional requirements . | Id | Requirement | Detail | . | UG-NFR-01 | Interoperability | Data exchange | . | UG-NFR-02 | Security and privacy | Adhere to data security standards, encrypt sensitive data, secure data transmission | . | UG-NFR-03 | Performance and scalability | Scalable to accommodate future increases in usage | . | UG-NFR-04 | Usability and user experience | Easy to use for various users | . | UG-NFR-05 | Compliance and regulation | Adhere to relevant regulations and standards | . | UG-NFR-06 | Training and support | Training resources and support to users for effective adoption and usage | . | UG-NFR-07 | Reliability and availability | Access when needed | . Other system features . Offline mode; parent or guardian portal; multilingual support; vaccine information and education; data migration and legacy system integration; data auditing and logging; mobile application; data quality checks; data sharing permissions; automated reporting to the National Drug Authority (NDA) and the Uganda Virus Research Institute (UVRI). Proposed EIR architecture . Child identification through integration with the birth registration system of the National Identification and Registration Authority (NIRA / vital registration system), feeding an EIR with a vaccine record module, scheduling and reminders, and data analytics and reporting. Users: health care providers, patients (via app or portal), and district and Ministry of Health staff. Edit this page on GitHub .

c9257bb5b9b7.title: Routine Schedule
c9257bb5b9b7.content: . The Uganda routine immunisation schedule, as published by the Ministry of Health and presented by UNEPI. Ages are the scheduled ages; every dose is given at that age or as soon as possible thereafter (see catch-up rules). Children . | Age | Vaccines | Diseases prevented | . | Birth | BCG, hepatitis B birth dose, OPV0 | Tuberculosis, hepatitis B, polio | . | 6 weeks (1.5 months) | OPV1, IPV1, DTP-HepB-Hib 1, PCV1, Rotavirus 1 | Polio, diphtheria, whooping cough, tetanus, hepatitis B, Haemophilus influenzae type b, pneumonia, meningitis, rotavirus diarrhoea | . | 10 weeks (2.5 months) | OPV2, DTP-HepB-Hib 2, PCV2, Rotavirus 2 | as at 6 weeks | . | 14 weeks (3.5 months) | OPV3, IPV2, DTP-HepB-Hib 3, PCV3, Rotavirus 3 | as at 6 weeks | . | 6 months | Malaria 1, Vitamin A | Malaria | . | 7 months | Malaria 2 | Malaria | . | 8 months | Malaria 3 | Malaria | . | 9 months | Measles-rubella 1 (MR1), Yellow fever | Measles, rubella, yellow fever | . | 12 months | Vitamin A, deworming | – | . | 18 months | Measles-rubella 2 (MR2), Malaria 4, Vitamin A | Measles, rubella, malaria | . | 24 months | Vitamin A | – | . | 10 years (girls) | HPV, 1 dose | Cancer of the cervix | . Vitamin A (6, 12, 18 and 24 months) and deworming (12 months) appear on the UNEPI schedule but are not vaccines; they are not part of the scheduling logic in this version (see open questions). The UNEPI schedule marks the hepatitis B birth dose, IPV1, the third rotavirus dose, yellow fever and MR2 as newly introduced, and malaria and HPV as yet to be introduced at the time of the presentation. The Ministry of Health poster includes malaria and single-dose HPV in the routine schedule. Women of child-bearing age (15 to 49 years) . | Dose | When | Vaccine | . | Td1 | At first contact | Tetanus-diphtheria | . | Td2 | 1 month after Td1 | Tetanus-diphtheria | . | Td3 | 6 months after Td2 | Tetanus-diphtheria | . | Td4 | 12 months after Td3 | Tetanus-diphtheria | . | Td5 | 12 months after Td4 | Tetanus-diphtheria | . Diseases targeted . UNEPI targets 14 vaccine-preventable diseases: tuberculosis, polio, diphtheria, pertussis (whooping cough), tetanus, hepatitis B, Haemophilus influenzae type b, pneumococcal disease, rotavirus gastroenteritis, measles, rubella, yellow fever, cancer of the cervix (HPV) and malaria. Messages to caregivers (Ministry of Health poster) . | Ask your health worker for your child’s next immunisation date. | Keep your child’s immunisation card safe and bring it every time you visit the health centre. | Report any side effects immediately to the health worker for proper clinical care. | Vaccines are safe, effective and free at all government health facilities. | . Ministry of Health toll-free line: 0800 100 066. Edit this page on GitHub .

2fdb3a9730d0.title: Service Delivery and Data Flow
2fdb3a9730d0.content: . Context from the UNEPI presentation. Service points . | Static: at the health facility. | Outreach: in the community. | School. | Immunity gap approaches: campaigns, routine, outbreak response (for example COVID-19). | . Client flow and integrated services at immunization sites . Immunization sessions are integrated with family planning, early infant diagnosis, HIV counselling and testing, nutrition assessment, vitamin A and deworming, postnatal care, and management of adverse events following immunization (AEFI). Data flow . Micro-plan → vaccination card → immunization child health register (ICHR) → tally sheet → HMIS 105 report → DHIS2 → monitoring chart. Support activities: data cleaning, data quality assessment, data review meetings, and RED/REC categorisation. Current digital systems for immunization . | System | Use | . | eCHIS | Community registries | . | eIDSR | Case-based surveillance | . | DHIS2 | Routine immunization reporting | . | EPIVAC | Campaigns | . | eMR | Facility workflows | . | ODK-X | Cold chain equipment | . | eLMIS | Logistics (approved) | . Other organisations UNEPI works with: National Drug Authority (NDA), Uganda Virus Research Institute (UVRI), National Medical Stores (NMS) and the National Identification and Registration Authority (NIRA). dca93174d2a2.title: Testing
dca93174d2a2.content: . Test patients follow the WHO DAK’s own layout: one directory per Logic library, input/tests/plandefinition/<Library>/<Library>.yaml, turned into FHIR test bundles by WHO’s tools/node/makeExample.js (npm run logic:examples; every file is built on each pull request). Each library’s Test Validation expression names, per test patient, the output that should hold, as the WHO libraries do. | Library | Test patients | Checks | . | IMMZD18SHepatitisBBirthDoseLogic | UGHepB01, UGHepB02 | birth dose due and expiring at 7 days; complete when given on day 3 | . | IMMZD18SPolioBOPVPlusIPVLogic | UGPolio01, UGPolio02 | IPV 1 due at 6 weeks; IPV 2 due at 14 weeks | . | IMMZD18SDTPOnTimeStartLogic | UGDTP01, UGDTP02 | DTP 1 at 6 weeks; no booster after the primary series | . | IMMZD18SMeaslesOngoingTransmissionLogic | UGMR01 | MCV2 due at 18 months | . | IMMZD18SMalariaLogic | UGMal01, UGMal02 | dose 1 at 6 months; dose 4 at 18 months | . | IMMZD18SHPVSingleDoseLogic | UGHPV01, UGHPV02 | girls at 10 years; not boys | . | IMMZD18SDTPTdWCBALogic | UGTd01–UGTd03 | Td 1 at first contact; Td 3 after Td 2; not men | . The CQL is compiled by the IG build (fhirbuild.yml, the WHO path). The WHO DAK toolchain has no runner that executes Test Validation on each change; the WHO checklist runs it by hand. That gap is reported to the platform rather than filled with a script in this repository. Edit this page on GitHub .
